title: The rain on the plants (Kern ch. 5)
hook: one rain falls on all plants, and each grows by its own nature

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples saw they had been the Buddha's heirs from the start, working for a wage when the treasure was theirs. Your line: heirs all along.

A summer storm doesn't check the garden plan before it rains. The same water lands on the tomatoes, the weeds by the fence, the old maple and the moss between the paving stones. And the next morning each has done something different with it. The tomato swells. The maple pushes out new leaves. The moss turns bright green. In chapter five of the Lotus, the Buddha answers the disciples' story, and he chooses weather.
screen: `A STORM WITH NO GARDEN PLAN.` → `SAME WATER, EVERY PLANT.` → `THE BUDDHA ANSWERS WITH WEATHER.`

segments.voice: In Kern's translation the Buddha tells Kasyapa of a great cloud that rises and spreads over the whole world, covering everything. Then it rains, everywhere at once, on grasses, bushes, herbs and trees, small, middle-sized and large, on every growing thing on mountains, in valleys and on the plains. The rain doesn't choose. It is one rain, the sutra says, of a single taste. But each plant takes up the water by its own nature and size, and grows, flowers and bears fruit in its own way. A blade of grass doesn't become an oak. It becomes more fully grass. The Buddha says he is like that cloud. He appears in the world and teaches gods, humans and all beings alike, and his teaching has one taste: the taste of release. He doesn't hold some back and pour more on others. He is equal toward everyone, the noble and the poor, those who keep the rules and those who break them, the quick and the slow. The difference is in the receiving. Each hears the teaching by their own capacity, and grows from there. This fits the last few days. In chapter two the teaching took many shapes. Here the source of all those shapes is one. The many ways belong to the hearers, like the many plants. The one goal belongs to the rain. It doesn't ask the grass to be a tree, or the tree to apologize for being tall. It just keeps raining on everyone, and lets each grow toward the same light in the way only it can.
screen: `A CLOUD OVER THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `ONE RAIN, EACH PLANT ITS OWN WAY.` · `ONE TASTE, EQUAL TO ALL.` · `MANY HEARERS, ONE SOURCE.` · then, large: `ONE RAIN, MANY PLANTS.`

segments.voice: If there's a plant near you, give it some water now, slowly, and watch the soil take it in; if not, picture one. Then breathe, each in-breath arriving like rain and each out-breath the plant quietly using it. No hurry; let it take what it can.
The rain on the plants. The Buddha's parable in chapter five: one rain of one taste falls on every plant, and each grows by its own nature. Today's word.
screen: `THE RAIN ON THE PLANTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one rain, many plants. One taste, and every plant its own way. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The parable of the medicinal plants in chapter five of the Lotus Sutra is taught in East Asian Buddhism as a picture of the Buddha's equal compassion: one teaching, received differently by each person according to their capacity.

chat.says: If the Buddha teaches everyone equally, why do people get such different things from it?
options: In the Lotus the teaching is one rain of one taste; each being takes it up by its own nature.
The rain is heavier in some places; the Lotus says he favors the quickest learners.
Only those who keep every rule can take in any of the teaching at all.
chat.meaning: Chapter five's cloud rains equally on every plant, and each grows by its own nature: one teaching, received by each by capacity.

Kasyapa.meaning: one of the Buddha's great disciples

Kern.meaning: the scholar whose English translation of the Lotus this path follows

Lotus.meaning: the Lotus Sutra, a Mahayana sutra of parables and visions

notes: Chapter 5 paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884); nothing quoted.

Check: the Buddha addresses Kasyapa; the cloud covering the world (Kern gives a cosmological scale, omitted); the plants of small, middle and large size; the 'one taste' of the teaching as the taste of deliverance or release; the Buddha's equality toward the noble and the low, the virtuous and the unvirtuous.
Kern's Sanskrit chapter 5 also contains the potter and the blind-man parables, absent from Kumarajiva's Chinese; not taught here. Keeper may want a note on the difference.
Original: oshadhi (ओषधी) as chapter-five title (Oshadhiparivarta); check spelling and stress.
